newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Stork denies blocking Fokker rebirth.
newsitem.headline: Stork denies blocking Fokker rebirth.

text.p: Industrial systems and services group Stork NV denied on Tuesday that it was standing in the way of a rebirth of bankrupt aircraft maker Fokker, as had been suggested in Dutch media reports.
"We are not blocking a Fokker restart," Stork chairman Jan Hovers told a news conference on his company's 1996 results.
If such a restart failed it would be because the new aircraft maker did not have a strong enough business plan and because suppliers and potential clients had insufficient confidence in it, he said.
"Stork has always been a constructive party (in the Fokker rebirth talks), also because as a supplier we have an economic interest in a sound restart," Hovers said.
He said there were many scenarios which had been and still were being discussed with various levels of Stork's involvement.

If Stork was required to invest risk bearing capital in a new Fokker company this involvement would be limited. Stork could certainly not put more than 10 percent of its shareholders' equity, which now totals 870 million guilders, in such a restarted company.
The fact that a new Fokker could not use substantial fiscal compensation claims, as was expected when the restart negotiations began, had not improved the chances of success.
A revived Fokker would also face major start up costs and take more than a year to be really in business.
"That certainly is an important factor in the considerations," Hovers said.
Fokker went bankrupt in early 1996 after its German parent DASA cut financial ties with the plane maker. Later, Stork bought Fokker Aviation, Fokker's profitable maintenance and components unit.
